content: Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is a serious disease affecting the central nervous system, caused by a virus transmitted through tick bites. This condition can result in severe neurological complications, including meningitis, meningoencephalitis, and meningoencephalomyelitis, which may lead to death. Currently, there is no available treatment for TBE, and vaccination remains the only preventive measure. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of TBE vaccines and their associated adverse effects. A comprehensive search for relevant studies was conducted in June 2008, utilizing databases such as the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and mRCT. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed. The study included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared TBE vaccines to placebo, control vaccines, no intervention, or different doses or schedules of the same vaccine. Two authors independently applied inclusion criteria, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias in each trial. Due to variations in the comparisons and outcomes of the included trials, a meta-analysis could not be performed. A total of 11 trials, corresponding to 10 published papers, were included in the analysis. These trials involved 8184 participants, comprising 6586 adults and 1598 children. The studies tested different versions of three TBE vaccines: IPVE, FSME-IMMUN, and Encepur. Among these, only three vaccines—Encepur Children, Encepur Adults, and FSME-IMMUN new—are currently licensed for use. None of the trials reported cases of clinical TBE as an outcome. However, all trials measured antibody titers (seroconversion) as an indicator of immune response. All tested vaccines demonstrated seroconversion rates exceeding 87%, indicating a strong immunogenic response. Systemic and local adverse effects were frequently reported, but none were classified as severe or life-threatening. In conclusion, TBE vaccines appear to be highly effective in inducing an immune response, as evidenced by high seroconversion rates. However, the correlation between seroconversion and actual clinical protection against TBE remains unclear. While adverse effects were commonly observed, they were generally mild and not life-threatening.
